report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Synopsis

At 02:47:12 on 12/08/2026, in the Stage 4 open pit at Bindarra Gold Mine, a 220 t class rigid [the other attendee 1], [the other attendee 1] 407, descending the main ramp empty, struck the right side of light vehicle LV-118 as it came out of the RL 312 dewatering spur. All times in this report are local time (UTC+8). The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] braked from 37 km/h and steered right, and the [the other attendee 1]'s front left hit LV-118 at 24 km/h. LV-118 was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side against the inner windrow. Its occupant, a grade control technician employed by a survey subcontractor, was on a third night shift at the mine, was conscious throughout, was extricated through the rear of the vehicle at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision, and was flown to the metropolitan trauma centre at 07:40. The injuries were a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax. LV-118 was destroyed, and the [the other attendee 1], damaged at the front left, returned to service on 14/08/2026. The Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes, the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours, and the occurrence was notified to the State Mines Inspectorate as a reportable injury.

The spur had been cut under a works order classed as routine earthworks, so no management of change record was raised and nothing was referred to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department or the technical services group. It was virtually certain that the intersection was left with no stop control or warning sign, while the available sight distance was 41 m against a stopping distance of 96 m. The traffic management plan required a positive call only at nine listed intersections, and the spur was not one of them. It is very likely that the plan's listing arrangement contributed, because the [the other attendee 1] had called at every listed intersection it passed that night. A collision awareness geofence extended in June 2026 also suppressed alerts at the spur, and operators did not know this. Probably this suppression contributed through the expectation that a quiet system meant an empty ramp, although that effect could not be measured. Neither driver knew of the other until the [the other attendee 1] came over the crest, six seconds before impact. The light vehicle drove out without stopping, which was very likely a contributing step, and the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s braking and steering within 1.4 seconds reduced the impact speed from 37 km/h to 24 km/h.

The roster of fourteen consecutive night shifts and the night shift extrication arrangement were unlikely to have influenced this occurrence, but both were found to increase risk. Whether airborne dust affected the sighting, and whether the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was fatigued, could not be determined either way.

The Mining Manager issued a site-wide direction on the night requiring a positive call at every Stage 4 intersection, closed the spur and, after survey, closed two further roads below the sight distance minimum. Tarrowen technical services began reporting suppressed collision alerts. Three recommendations are open, covering works orders that create new intersections, a route onto the positive-call list between annual reviews, and changes to suppression geofences.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s role title as the report should state it]

Factual information

History of the occurrence

The RL 312 dewatering spur was a 240 m access road to bore DW-14 in the Stage 4 pit at Bindarra Gold Mine. It was cut under works order WO-26-4471, raised on 28/07/2026 and recorded as completed on 31/07/2026. The spur was first used by light vehicles on 02/08/2026, when bore DW-14 was energised. The works log records the "ROAD CLOSED - CONSTRUCTION" sign at the spur mouth as removed that day, and nothing was installed in its place.

At about 22:10 on 04/08/2026 a dewatering technician came out of the spur in front of a [the other attendee 1] descending the main ramp about 60 m away. The technician reversed back into the spur and let the [the other attendee 1] pass. The technician submitted hazard report HAZ-2026-0917 at 23:48 the same night, and the Dewatering Superintendent closed it on 06/08/2026. The risk rating was reduced from Medium to Low on closure. On 09/08/2026 a site access card was issued to the light vehicle driver after a 20 minute gatehouse briefing, and the first of the driver's three night shifts at Bindarra began that evening.

On the night of 11 to 12/08/2026 the Stage 4 pit returned from the crib break at 02:22:41, when dispatch called the units back to work. [the other attendee 1] 407 began the first of its post-crib cycles at 02:22:53. At about 02:45 to about 02:47 the light vehicle, LV-118, left the collar of bore DW-14 and drove the 240 m of spur towards the main ramp. This time is estimated from the light vehicle driver's account and the length of the spur. The driver's own recollection of the time was later than the recorded collision and was not used. The light vehicle driver had completed a grade control pickup at the bore collar. No one else in the pit knew the light vehicle was there.

[the other attendee 1] 407 was descending the main ramp empty. Its last steady data point, at 02:47:06.0, was 37 km/h at RL 317, 53 m above the spur mouth. At 02:47:07.4, 38.5 m above the mouth, service brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds, the retarder went to maximum and 14 degrees of right steering was applied. At 02:47:09.2 the collision awareness system logged a proximity event with the light vehicle at 21.4 m and suppressed the alert. The light vehicle driver said that LV-118 slowed at the spur mouth, that the driver looked right up the ramp, saw nothing and drove out, turning right to go up the ramp. The driver put the speed at about 25 km/h and did not believe the vehicle came to a complete stop. The driver first said "stopped" and corrected it to "slowed" on read-back.

The [the other attendee 1]'s front left struck the right side of LV-118 at 02:47:12.0, at 24 km/h, 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth. The [the other attendee 1] pushed LV-118 18.4 m down the ramp and it rolled onto its left side against the inner windrow. The [the other attendee 1] stopped at about 02:47:19, 19 m below the intersection, with the park brake applied.

The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s first call was at 02:47:41. Dispatch stopped all Stage 4 traffic at 02:48:01, which was 49 seconds after the collision and 20 seconds after the first call. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was told to stay in the cab until the ramp was clear above and below, and was released at 02:48:44. The emergency response team was paged at 02:48. At 02:49:30 the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] reported that the driver was conscious and talking but could not get out because the door was against the ground. The night shift supervisor, who had been at the ROM pad, said that they were on scene about five minutes after the call. The first response vehicle entered the pit at 02:51 and reached the scene at 02:54. The paramedic's primary survey was complete and the extrication plan made at 02:58. The second responder arrived with the hydraulic rescue tool at 03:07. The driver was extricated through the rear of the vehicle at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision. The driver reached the surface medical facility at 03:41 and was flown to the metropolitan trauma centre at 07:40.

The occurrence notification, ORR-OCC-2026-0332, was raised at 03:26 on 12/08/2026. It lists these immediate actions:

  • The Stage 4 pit was stood down, the main ramp was closed below RL 340 and the spur was barricaded and closed to all traffic.
  • Both vehicles were isolated and left in position, and the scene was photographed and surveyed before recovery.
  • The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] and the shift supervisor were stood down for the rest of the shift, and both tested negative for drugs and alcohol.
  • Fleet management system and collision awareness system data were downloaded from the [the other attendee 1] at 09:30 and provided to the investigation unopened.
  • The Mining Manager issued a site-wide direction at 05:10 requiring a positive call on the pit channel before entering any Stage 4 intersection, listed in the plan or not, until further notice.

The Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes and the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours. The occurrence was notified to the State Mines Inspectorate as a reportable injury.

Injuries to persons

The light vehicle driver, the only occupant of LV-118, was seriously injured. The injuries were a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax. The driver was conscious throughout and was treated at the surface medical facility before air evacuation.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was injured]

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any drug and alcohol result for the light vehicle driver]

Damage

LV-118 was destroyed. Its roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting and was not breached. The driver's seatbelt was found fastened, with loading marks on the webbing. The 4.5 m amber beacon whip was sheared at its base and recovered 9 m from the vehicle, and its lamp worked when tested. Damage to LV-118 was concentrated on the right side from the B pillar forward.

Damage to the [the other attendee 1] was confined to the front left bumper, the left mudguard and the lower two steps of the access ladder, with nothing above the bumper line. The [the other attendee 1] returned to service on 14/08/2026.

Personnel information

The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] had 14 months at Bindarra, 4 years 2 months with Tarrowen Mining Services, 7 years on 220 t class rigid trucks and 11 years in open pit mining. The [the other attendee 1]'s verification of competency on the 220 t class unit was issued in 06/2025 and was current. The annual refresher was completed in 02/2026 and the site general induction in 06/2025. The training file shows no traffic management refresher since the general induction. The induction's traffic management module is a 23 slide package that names the nine Appendix B intersections and does not cover what to do at an unlisted intersection. No training record anywhere on site, for any person, covers the collision awareness system's suppression geofences.

The occurrence was on night 10 of a 14 night swing, 8 hours 47 minutes into a 12 hour 30 minute shift. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s voluntary sleep record gives 6 hours 30 minutes of sleep in the day before the occurrence and between 5 and 7 hours on each of the preceding nine days. Site access records confirm that the previous nine shifts were worked in sequence, with none extended beyond 12 hours 40 minutes.

The light vehicle driver was a grade control technician employed by a survey subcontractor, Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical. The driver completed a two hour Hallorn online general induction on 24/07/2026. The Bindarra site access card was issued on 09/08/2026 against Hallorn's recognition agreement, after the 20 minute gatehouse briefing on muster points, speed limits and personal protective equipment. The driver worked three night shifts at Bindarra, on 09/08, 10/08 and 11/08. There is no record of the Bindarra site-specific supplement being issued, completed or signed for, and no record of the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment. The gatehouse neither requires nor asked for either. The light vehicle driver's account was that the driver had never heard of the pit driving assessment and had never seen the traffic management plan.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the Bindarra site-specific supplement was issued to the light vehicle driver]

The night shift supervisor had 19 years in open pit mining, 8 years with Tarrowen Mining Services and 2 years 6 months in the role. On night shift the supervisor was responsible for the [the other attendee 1] fleet, the excavators, the ancillary fleet, the dozers and the dispatch, and was not responsible for the dewatering crew, the survey contractor or any other light vehicle in the pit. The supervisor worked the same 14 night pattern as the crews supervised, and was also on night 10 of 14.

Equipment information

The [the other attendee 1] was a 220 t class rigid [the other attendee 1] commissioned in 03/2021, with 31,480 engine hours. Its last 500 hour service was on 28/07/2026 with no defects carried. The monthly brake performance test on 03/08/2026 gave a mean net deceleration of 0.80 m/s2 in the empty condition on a 9 per cent descending grade. A test on 14/08/2026, before the unit returned to service, gave 0.82 m/s2 on the same grade. The pre-start check sheet for 11/08/2026 was complete and recorded no defects. No defect was raised against the retarder, service brakes, park brake, lighting, mirrors, cameras or cab glass in the twelve months before the occurrence.

LV-118 was a 4WD utility, in service since 02/2024, with 61,200 km. Its last periodic service was on 17/07/2026, 4,100 km before the occurrence. It was fitted with a certified roll-over protection structure, a 4.5 m amber beacon whip, reflective marking to the site standard and a UHF radio. The inspection sheet for the week of 09/08/2026 recorded all items serviceable. LV-118 was not dispatched and carried no fleet management system. Its collision awareness transponder was a passive tag.

The collision awareness system on the [the other attendee 1] fleet operated at Level 8, [the other attendee 1] advisory. Level 9, automated intervention, was available on the fleet and was not enabled at Bindarra. Advisory alerts were raised when a vehicle tag entered the 60 m detection ring at a closing rate above 10 km/h, except inside a suppression geofence. Inside a suppression geofence no alert was raised at any range, and the system logged a proximity event only once the range fell below 25 m.

Geofence S4-LOAD was drawn on 14/03/2025 around the Stage 4 loading face to stop nuisance alerts between the excavator, the trucks under it and the service vehicles working there. It was extended northward on 09/06/2026 when the loading face advanced, which carried the boundary up the main ramp for the first time. The extended boundary lay 180 m up-ramp of the RL 312 intersection, and the intersection, cut seven weeks later, lay inside the suppressed area. The extension was made by the contractor's technical services group as a system configuration task. It is not recorded in the traffic management plan and was not reviewed against it.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the size of the S4-LOAD extension on 09/06/2026, because the configuration gives the new boundary and not the old one]

The fleet management system in-cab map for the Stage 4 pit was last published on 24/07/2026. It does not contain the RL 312 spur, so the in-cab display showed the main ramp with no intersection at RL 312 on the night. Publishing a revised road network is a survey task raised by a management of change record, and no such record exists for the spur.

Site information

At RL 312 the main ramp runs approximately north-west on a 9.1 per cent descending grade and is 24 m wide between windrows. On 12/08/2026 its surface was dry and well maintained, with no corrugation or loose material beyond the normal running surface. Traffic keeps left, so a descending [the other attendee 1] runs on the open, pit side of the road.

The spur joins the ramp on a descending [the other attendee 1]'s left, on the inside of a left-hand bend, at an included angle of 71 degrees. It meets the ramp 34 m below a convex grade break, where the descent steepens, which the crews call the crest. LV-118 was turning right out of the spur to go up the ramp, which took it across the descending lane with its right side towards the [the other attendee 1]. The spur was cut under WO-26-4471, which classified the work as routine earthworks within the approved Stage 4 design. The works order recorded management of change as not required under ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3, and its handover field read "N/A".

Mine survey pickup SUR-26-1188, made on 13/08/2026, gave these measurements:

  • A [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] seated at an eye height of 5.80 m first has line of sight to the spur mouth at 41 m.
  • The top of the 4.5 m beacon whip of a light vehicle approaching the mouth is in view from the same eye height from 53 m, over the grade break and above the windrow, while the vehicle's body is not.
  • A driver at the spur mouth, at an eye height of 1.45 m, first has line of sight to a descending [the other attendee 1] at 38 m.
  • The 1.6 m inner windrow stands between the spur and the ramp for the last 25 m of the spur's approach and takes the [the other attendee 1]'s lower body out of view before that.
  • The stopping distance of a 220 t class [the other attendee 1] travelling empty at the posted 40 km/h on a 9 per cent descending grade, calculated with the manufacturer's data and a 1.5 second response, is 96 m.

The survey recorded that the intersection does not meet clause 6.2 of the traffic management plan on either limb.

At the time of the occurrence the intersection carried no intersection warning sign on either ramp approach, no give-way or stop control at the spur mouth, no delineation, reflective marker posts or windrow gap markers, and no posted speed for the spur. The scene examination recovered these marks, measured from the up-ramp edge of the spur mouth:

  • A continuous braked scuff from the [the other attendee 1]'s left front tyre began 38.5 m up-ramp of the mouth and ran 58 m to the [the other attendee 1]'s resting position. It deviated 1.4 m to the right over its first 20 m.
  • The impact position was 6.2 m into the ramp from the mouth and 3.1 m out from the toe of the inner windrow.
  • A continuous gouge ran 18.4 m down-ramp from the impact position. It changed at 11.2 m from tyre scuff to body panel gouge, which is where the vehicle went over.
  • LV-118 came to rest on its left side against the inner windrow, facing down-ramp, 18.4 m below the impact position, with right-side glass and mirror fragments from 4.8 m to 14 m down-ramp of the impact position.

Meteorology, light and surface

The occurrence was in darkness. There is no fixed lighting anywhere in the Stage 4 pit, and the only lighting is vehicle lighting and the light plants at the loading face, 1.1 km away and out of sight behind the crest. Moonset was at 23:18 the previous evening. The Bindarra met station at the ROM pad recorded wind from the south-east at 8 km/h, a temperature of 9 degrees and no precipitation. The last rainfall at the site was 26 days before the occurrence. The investigator examined the ramp at 06:20 and found it dry throughout, with no damp patches, ponding or greasy film at or above the intersection.

The water cart log records the main ramp between RL 280 and RL 400 as last watered at 01:10, 1 hour 37 minutes before the occurrence. The standing night shift instruction is a ramp pass every 90 minutes, so a pass was 7 minutes overdue. The fixed dust monitor on the RL 328 bench beside the ramp, 180 m up-ramp of the intersection and above the grade break, logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre in the 02:40 to 02:50 interval. The shift mean was 88 and the site trigger is 250. The reading is a measure of airborne particulate at the monitor head. Nothing at Bindarra measures visibility, and no measurement exists of what could be seen from either cab on the night.

The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] said there was "some hanging around" on the descent, that the cart had been through earlier but "it dries out", and that the [the other attendee 1] could not say whether it made a difference. The light vehicle driver's account was that the air was clear and that the ramp surface and the windrow could be seen.

Recorded information

The pit channel was recorded continuously as RAD-2026-0332, and the investigator listened to the whole period from the return from crib to two minutes after the collision. The recording's clock was checked against the fleet management system to within 0.4 seconds. [the other attendee 1] 407 called at each listed intersection it passed, and dispatch acknowledged each call. It called at the RL 360 crossover going up at 02:28:10, at the ROM pad turn-off at 02:37:20, and at the RL 360 crossover coming down at 02:46:21:

  • "407, three-sixty crossover, empty, going down through." (pit channel recording, 02:46:21)

Dispatch replied "Copy 407." at 02:46:24, 51 seconds before the collision. The recording contains no transmission by either vehicle about the RL 312 spur, the dewatering bore, or a light vehicle being anywhere in the Stage 4 pit. LV-118 made no transmission on the channel that shift beyond logging on at 18:04 at the start of shift. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s first call after the collision was at 02:47:41:

  • "Dispatch, 407. I've hit a light vehicle on the ramp at three-twelve. I've hit a light vehicle. He's on his side." (pit channel recording, 02:47:41, marked in the extract as raised voice)

The fleet management system download, TRW-TS-2026-114, shows the [the other attendee 1] at 39 km/h at RL 384 at 02:45:58 and 38 km/h at RL 351 at 02:46:31. It records 1.4 seconds between the last steady data point and the first rise in brake pressure. Mean deceleration from brake application to collision was 0.78 m/s2 net of the grade, from 37 km/h to 24 km/h in 4.6 seconds over 39 m of road, against 0.80 m/s2 in the 03/08/2026 test. The download records that on a 9.1 per cent descent gravity takes about 0.88 m/s2 off what the brakes produce. The accelerometer logged 1.9 g longitudinal at the impact. The impact and the push took the [the other attendee 1] to about 20 km/h, and it came to rest about seven seconds after the collision. The download records that the retarder and service brakes performed as specified throughout. It also records that with no braking the collision speed would have been 37 km/h.

The collision awareness event log for 11/08/2026 (UTC) records the proximity event at 02:47:09.2 local time, 2.8 seconds before the collision. It gave the range as 21.4 m and the closing speed as 32 km/h, in zone S4-LOAD, with the alert:

  • "alert SUPPRESSED (geofence)" (collision awareness system event log)

The log then records the impact at 02:47:12.000 at 1.9 g longitudinal. A second proximity event follows at 02:47:12.1, range 0.0 m, also suppressed.

The twelve month alert statistics to 11/08/2026 show that the [the other attendee 1] raised 1,684 advisory alerts, every one outside the S4-LOAD geofence and none inside it. Across the Stage 4 [the other attendee 1] fleet, 68 proximity events were logged inside the geofence and suppressed. Nine of them involved a light vehicle tag on the main ramp below the geofence boundary, and all nine are dated after 09/06/2026. Before the June extension the boundary did not reach the ramp, and the system was live there. The suppressed events are recorded in the system and visible to anyone who queries it. The technical services group's standing report covers alert counts and system health and does not report suppressed events.

Organisational and management information

External guidance

Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14, revision 4 (2021), was issued by the State Mines Inspectorate under regulation 6.22 of the Mining Operations Safety Regulations 2018. Compliance with the guideline is one way of discharging the regulation, which requires that the [the other attendee 1] "shall manage the risks arising from the interaction of vehicles at the mine". The guideline provides:

  • The traffic management plan "shall be reviewed at intervals not exceeding twelve months, and following any significant change to the mine's road network, vehicle fleet or operating pattern." (MSG-14 clause 3.2)
  • "The plan is a site document. It is not approved by, and need not be submitted to, the Inspectorate, except on request following an occurrence or an inspection." (MSG-14 clause 3.5)
  • The [the other attendee 1] nominates "the intersections, crossings and other interaction zones at the mine at which positive communication between vehicles is required before entry, and shall record them in the plan." (MSG-14 clause 5.1)
  • "Detectability may be provided by line of sight, elevated marking, radio communication, a proximity detection system, or a combination of these." (MSG-14 clause 5.4)

The guideline does not define "significant change" and gives no example of one. It does not say who nominates the interaction zones at clause 5.1 or on what basis, and it sets no minimum. It does not say which of the five means at clause 5.4 must be provided, or how many.

The traffic management plan

The Bindarra traffic management plan, BIN-TMP-004 revision 7, was issued on 12/11/2025 and its next review was due on 12/11/2026. Its owner is the Mining Manager, Orrabinda Resources. It provides:

  • "Light vehicles shall give way to heavy vehicles at all times and in all circumstances." (clause 4.1)
  • "A positive call shall be made on the relevant pit channel before entering any intersection listed at Appendix B, and entry shall not be made until the call is acknowledged or the channel is confirmed clear." (clause 4.3.1)
  • "At intersections not listed at Appendix B, vehicles shall give way in accordance with clause 4.1. No call is required." (clause 4.3.2)
  • "At every intersection, the available sight distance shall be not less than the stopping distance of the largest vehicle using the road at the posted speed, and in no case less than 120 m. Where this cannot be achieved, the intersection shall be controlled by a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller." (clause 6.2)
  • "Every intersection shown on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1 shall be provided with an intersection warning sign 50 m in advance on each approach, a give-way control on the minor road, and delineation at the mouth." (clause 6.4)
  • "This plan shall be reviewed annually, and following any significant change to the mine's road network." (clause 9.1)

Appendix B lists nine intersections: the ROM pad turn-off, the RL 360 crossover, the Stage 2 ramp junction, the Stage 2 dump access, the Stage 3 ramp junction, the workshop apron entry, the explosives magazine access, the raw water pump station access and the light vehicle parking bay at RL 400. The RL 312 spur is not among them. The note to Appendix B provides that the appendix is reviewed and reissued at the annual review, and that an intersection is added where it appears on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1 and the review assesses it as requiring positive communication. Schedule 1 is dated 12/11/2025, is reissued at the annual review and does not show the spur. No provision in the plan allows an intersection to be added to Appendix B or Schedule 1 between annual reviews, and none requires a new road to be referred to the plan's owner when it is cut. Appendix B is reproduced on a laminated board in each crib room, and the board in the Stage 4 crib room is the 12/11/2025 issue. Clause 6.4 applies to intersections shown on Schedule 1.

Annual reviews were completed on 14/11/2023, 10/11/2024 and 12/11/2025. No out-of-cycle review under clause 9.1 has been carried out in the plan's eleven year history. The survey department's road register shows 14 new roads cut in the Stage 4 pit since the 12/11/2025 review. Of these, 3 were cut under a management of change record and were referred to the plan's owner, and 11 were cut under a works order and none was referred.

Management of change

Procedure ORR-PRO-022 revision 3 provides:

  • "A management of change record shall be raised before any of the following: a change to the mine's road network; the introduction of a new vehicle type; a change to a pit design; a change to a documented control." (clause 5.2)
  • "Clause 5.2 does not apply to routine earthworks carried out under a works order within an approved pit design, where no new plant or vehicle type is introduced. Such work is managed under the works order." (clause 5.3)
  • Where a record is raised, the change owner completes the impact assessment at Schedule 2, "which includes referral to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system configuration." (clause 5.4)

The three referrals at clause 5.4 exist only inside the management of change record. The works order form at Schedule 4 has no equivalent fields and no referral of any kind. WO-26-4471 carried no scope for signage, no survey pickup of the new intersection, no referral to the plan's owner, no request to publish a revised road network and no review of the geofences. It was raised by a Mining Engineer on 28/07/2026 and approved by the Mining Superintendent on 29/07/2026.

Contractor management and access

Contractor Management Standard ORR-STD-009 revision 5 provides:

  • "A contractor's own general induction may be accepted as equivalent to the Bindarra general induction where the contractor holds a current recognition agreement with Orrabinda Resources." (clause 7.3)
  • "Equivalence under 7.3 does not extend to the Bindarra site-specific supplement, or to the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment, which shall be completed at site by every person who will drive a vehicle in an operating pit and shall not be substituted." (clause 7.4)
  • "The engaging department is responsible for verifying that 7.4 has been completed before a site access card is issued." (clause 7.5)

Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical has held a recognition agreement since 2023. The gatehouse issues site access cards against the recognition agreement alone, holds no record of the supplement or the pit driving assessment and is not asked for one. Nothing in the access card system distinguishes a person who may drive in an operating pit from a person who may not. The night shift supervisor said there is no permit, radio call-in, board or check at the pit entry, and that anyone with a site access card can drive in.

Earlier reports of the same type of interaction

Four hazard reports raised at Bindarra in the 24 months to 11/08/2026 describe a light vehicle and a [the other attendee 1] meeting unexpectedly at an intersection. The first three, from 03/2025, 09/2025 and 02/2026, concern three different locations, none listed at Appendix B. The fourth is HAZ-2026-0917. Each was closed by the department that received it within three days, with an entry that the crew had been reminded to take care and that heavy vehicles have right of way. None was referred to the plan's owner, and none resulted in a change to Appendix B, to Schedule 1 or to any physical control.

The dewatering technician's report, HAZ-2026-0917, was submitted at 23:48 on 04/08/2026, seven days before the occurrence, with a submitter's risk rating of Medium. It included these statements:

  • "The problem is you cannot see up the ramp from that road." (HAZ-2026-0917)
  • "I do not think they know the road is there." (HAZ-2026-0917)

It also said there was no sign on the ramp, no give way on the spur side and that the closed sign had been taken away. The Dewatering Superintendent's closure entry of 06/08/2026 included:

  • "reminded them to take care entering the main ramp" (HAZ-2026-0917 closure entry)
  • "No further action required. Closed." (HAZ-2026-0917 closure entry)

The report was not referred to the mining department, the contractor, the survey department or the traffic management plan owner, and the risk rating on closure was Low.

Roster and emergency response

The contractor's Stage 4 [the other attendee 1] roster is 14 nights on and 7 off, 18:00 to 06:30, a 12 hour 30 minute shift with a 30 minute crib. The contractor's fatigue management standard sets a maximum of 14 consecutive night shifts and a minimum 10 hour break, and both limits were met.

The Bindarra night shift is rostered with one qualified mines rescue paramedic, who was at the surface medical facility. The second responder is required before any extrication begins. The second responder is called in from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse, and travels in the second response vehicle, which is garaged there and carries the hydraulic rescue tool. The times on the night are given above.
