Analysis

This analysis follows the chain from the change to the mine's road network to the injury, taking each condition in the order in which it acted on the next.

What the analysis had to settle

The analysis had to settle why a light vehicle and a descending [the other attendee 1] reached the RL 312 intersection together, each unknown to the other until six seconds before the impact. It also had to settle which of the conditions behind that were within the mine's control, and to separate them from conditions that were examined and did not bear on the occurrence.

The equipment was serviceable. The monthly brake performance test on 03/08/2026 gave a mean deceleration of 0.80 m/s2 net, and the test repeated on 14/08/2026 before the [the other attendee 1] returned to service gave 0.82. The occurrence download gave 0.78 over the 4.6 seconds of braking. Service brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds and the retarder went to maximum. The pre-start sheet for 11/08/2026 recorded no defects, and no brake, retarder, park brake, lighting, mirror, camera or cab glass defect had been raised in the previous twelve months. The evidence therefore did not support a brake shortfall, and it was very unlikely that the service brakes delivered less than their tested deceleration. LV-118 was also serviceable, and the lamp of its beacon worked when tested after recovery.

The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s qualifications and recency were not in question. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] had seven years on 220 t class trucks, a verification of competency on the type issued in 06/2025 and current, and an annual refresher completed in 02/2026. The notification records that the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was tested for drugs and alcohol after the occurrence and that the result was negative.

The road surface played no part. The met station recorded no precipitation on the night and the last rainfall at the site was 26 days earlier. The water cart's last pass on the section was at 01:10, and the investigator found the ramp dry throughout at 06:20, with no damp patches, ponding or greasy film. The braked tyre scuff ran continuously for 58 m with no sign of a locked or sliding wheel, and the deceleration achieved matched the [the other attendee 1]'s tested figures on the same dry grade. It was very unlikely that the ramp was wet or slippery.

Two matters could not be settled and are discussed separately below. They are whether the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was fatigued on the approach and whether airborne dust affected the sighting.

How the intersection came to exist without a control

The mine's procedure for management of change required that "A management of change record shall be raised before any of the following: a change to the mine's road network". It also provided that "Clause 5.2 does not apply to routine earthworks carried out under a works order within an approved pit design, where no new plant or vehicle type is introduced." Works order WO-26-4471 was raised on 28/07/2026 and approved on 29/07/2026. It cut 240 m of access road to dewatering bore DW-14 at RL 312, completed on 31/07/2026. The order classified the work as routine earthworks within the approved Stage 4 design, recorded management of change as not required under clause 5.3, and left its handover field reading "N/A".

The exclusion mattered because of what a management of change record carried. Clause 5.4 required referral to the traffic management plan owner, to the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and to the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system configuration. The works order form has no equivalent fields, so none of the three referrals was made.

The in-cab road network was last published on 24/07/2026, before the spur was cut, so it showed the main ramp with no intersection at RL 312 on the night. Publishing a revised network is a survey task raised by a management of change record, and none existed for the spur. The S4-LOAD suppression geofence had already been carried up the ramp on 09/06/2026 and covered the point where the spur joined it. The construction sign at the spur mouth was removed on 02/08/2026, the day the bore was energised and the spur first used, and nothing replaced it.

The comparison within Stage 4 shows that the gap was general. Of the 14 new roads cut since the plan review of 12/11/2025, the three raised under a management of change record were all referred to the plan owner, and none of the eleven raised under a works order was.

The contrary evidence was that a referral is not a control. The plan owner might have left the spur to the annual review, and no out-of-cycle review had been held in the plan's eleven years. However, a referral would have put a survey in front of the plan owner showing the intersection failing the sight distance rule, and would have reached the group that configures the geofences. On the evidence, the works order route was virtually certain to have been used, and it is very likely that had the change gone through management of change, the referrals would have sent the intersection to the people able to give it a stop control, a place on the in-cab map and a review of the geofence. This was a causal factor.

The sight line and the missing controls

The plan required that "At every intersection, the available sight distance shall be not less than the stopping distance of the largest vehicle using the road at the posted speed, and in no case less than 120 m." Where that could not be achieved, the intersection "shall be controlled by a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller." The survey of 13/08/2026 gave 41 m available at the spur against a stopping distance of 96 m for an empty 220 t class [the other attendee 1] at the posted 40 km/h on a 9 per cent descending grade. The intersection met neither limb of clause 6.2, so the stop control requirement applied.

The geometry explained why the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] saw so little. The spur mouth lies 34 m below a convex grade break. From an eye height of 5.80 m the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] first had line of sight to the mouth at 41 m, and to the top of the 4.5 m beacon whip on an approaching light vehicle at 53 m. The vehicle body was not in view. A driver at the mouth, at an eye height of 1.45 m, first had line of sight to a descending [the other attendee 1] at 38 m, and the 1.6 m inner windrow took the [the other attendee 1]'s lower body out of view before that. The occurrence was in darkness with no fixed lighting in the pit.

A [the other attendee 1] at 37 km/h needed about 68 m on brakes alone at the recorded 0.78 m/s2, against the 53 m at which the beacon first became visible. With twice the sight line, the same 1.4 second response and the same braking would have stopped the [the other attendee 1] short of the spur. A sight line is only hazardous once something is in it, and the preceding conditions put a vehicle there, so the short sight line very likely contributed to the collision. This was a causal factor.

The signage requirement was a different matter. Clause 6.4 required a warning sign 50 m in advance on each approach, a give-way control on the minor road and delineation at the mouth, but only at intersections "shown on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1". The spur was not on that drawing, so clause 6.4 did not apply to it. The requirement that did apply, clause 6.2, called for a stop control. At the time of the occurrence the intersection had no warning sign on either ramp approach, no stop or give-way control, no delineation and no posted speed.

The absence had been described in writing seven days earlier. At about 22:10 on 04/08/2026 a dewatering technician came out of the spur in front of a [the other attendee 1] about 60 m up the ramp, reversed back into the spur and let the [the other attendee 1] pass. The technician's hazard report said "I do not think they know the road is there." The report was closed on 06/08/2026 with a reminder to the crew and a lower risk rating, and the sight line and controls were left as they were. The technician's response shows that a driver who saw the [the other attendee 1] in time could let it pass.

The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s account supports the same reading. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] thought the spur was still closed, noticed that the closed sign was gone without thinking about it, and said: "If there'd been a sign on my side of that crest I'd have been at twenty and I'd have been looking for him." A stop control at the mouth would have held the light vehicle there, and the [the other attendee 1] was inside the 38 m view from about 02:47:07.4, nearly two seconds before the light vehicle reached the mouth at 02:47:09.2.

Several points weighed the other way. A stop line is only as good as the look from it, and 38 m gave about four seconds of a [the other attendee 1] at 37 km/h, a thin margin even from a standstill. The driver was already slowing and looking, and the effect of a warning sign on the [the other attendee 1] rests on the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s own view after the event. A sign at an intersection absent from the in-cab map would also have been a single cue. Even so, it is likely that the absence of a stop control and warning signs contributed by leaving both drivers without the prompt that would have changed what each did. This too was a causal factor.

Why the positive-call defence did not apply

The plan required "A positive call ... before entering any intersection listed at Appendix B" and, at intersections not listed, that "No call is required." Appendix B listed nine intersections. Its note provided that the appendix was reviewed and reissued at the annual review, and that an intersection was added where it appeared on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1 and the review assessed it as requiring positive communication. Schedule 1 was dated 12/11/2025 and was reissued only at the annual review. Nothing in the plan allowed an intersection to be added between reviews, and nothing required a new road to be referred to the plan's owner when it was cut. The spur was on neither document, and the next review was due on 12/11/2026, three months after the collision.

The pit channel shows how the arrangement worked in practice. The [the other attendee 1] called and was acknowledged at the RL 360 crossover going up at 02:28:10, at the ROM pad turn-off at 02:37:20, and at the RL 360 crossover coming down at 02:46:21, 51 seconds before the collision. It made no call at the spur. LV-118 made no transmission after logging on at 18:04 at the start of the shift. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1], the light vehicle driver and the night shift supervisor each described the same practice independently, that calls were made at the nine listed intersections and nowhere else. The supervisor said they wanted a call but had never corrected anyone for not calling elsewhere, and that requiring calls everywhere would make the channel unusable.

Had the spur been listed, it is very likely that the call would have been made, because the [the other attendee 1] called at every listed intersection it passed that night and the light vehicle was on the channel. The contrary point is that a call gives knowledge and not separation, and that a call made but not acknowledged still leaves a driver deciding whether to go. The mine's own defence against this interaction was not armed at this intersection by its own terms. This was a causal factor.

For the individual absence of calls on the night, the evidence is the same recording. No call was required of either driver, so their conduct matched the plan. It is likely that the absence of a call from either vehicle contributed, because a call from either would have been heard by the other, by dispatch and by the supervisor, who did not know a light vehicle was in the pit. The same limit applies, since two vehicles would still have had to resolve who went first over a short sight line. This too was a causal factor.

The external guideline sat behind the plan. MSG-14 clause 3.2 required the plan to be reviewed at intervals not exceeding twelve months "and following any significant change to the mine's road network, vehicle fleet or operating pattern", but defined neither the term nor an example. Clause 5.1 required the mine to nominate the intersections at which positive communication was required, with no minimum and no basis. Clause 3.5 provided that the plan is a site document, not approved by the Inspectorate except on request after an occurrence. Bindarra's plan met the guideline on its face, because it had been reviewed within twelve months and nominated nine zones, so the mine was not in breach.

The guideline's effect was therefore limited. A defined trigger for review and a stated basis for nomination would have given a new intersection on a [the other attendee 1] road a route onto the call list between annual reviews. However, the mine could have held an out-of-cycle review under its own clause 9.1 at any time, and could have listed every intersection it had. Bindarra did not fail to act because the guideline was vague. Nothing inside the mine put the question in front of the plan's owner. The guideline probably contributed by making inaction the default, but this is the narrowest of the organisational conclusions in this analysis, and it was a causal factor.

Alerts suppressed by the geofence

The collision awareness system on the [the other attendee 1] operated at Level 8, advisory only. Level 9 intervention was available on the fleet and was not enabled at Bindarra. Advisory alerts were raised when a tag entered the 60 m ring above a 10 km/h closing rate, but "Inside a suppression geofence no alert is raised at any range, and the system logs a proximity event only once the range falls below 25 m."

The S4-LOAD geofence was drawn on 14/03/2025 around the loading face to stop nuisance alerts. It was extended northward on 09/06/2026 as a configuration task by the contractor's technical services group, which carried the boundary up the main ramp for the first time, 180 m up-ramp of where the spur was later cut. The extension was not recorded in the traffic management plan or reviewed against it. The log shows the proximity event at 02:47:09.2 at 21.4 m, closing at 32 km/h, with the alert suppressed.

The operators did not know. It is almost certain that no [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] on the fleet knew the system was off on the ramp, but this rests on two accounts and on the absence of any training record or notice, and no other [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was asked. The supervisor knew the system was off at the dig from about the middle of 2025 and did not know the boundary had been extended. The supervisor told the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] after the collision. No training record anywhere on site, for any person, covers the geofences.

The suppressed events had been recorded throughout and nobody had looked. In the twelve months to 11/08/2026 the [the other attendee 1] raised 1,684 advisory alerts, every one outside the geofence. Across the Stage 4 [the other attendee 1] fleet 68 proximity events inside it were suppressed, nine of them a light vehicle on the main ramp below the boundary, all after 09/06/2026. The standing technical services report did not include suppressed events. For the first ten months of the period the ramp was outside the geofence, so a quiet system there meant an empty ramp. From June it was quiet whatever was on the road.

The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] described the resulting expectation. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] had never had an alert on that ramp in fourteen months and took it that "if the thing's quiet, the road's empty." On a ramp that showed no intersection on the screen and none on the road, the expectation gave one less reason to think anyone could be there. It is likely that the suppression contributed in this way, but the effect is real and cannot be measured.

The evidence against was that the alert itself would have bought nothing. Unsuppressed, it would have sounded when the light vehicle's tag entered the 60 m ring, at about 02:47:06.5, half a second after the beacon came into view and about a second before the brakes went on. It would have told the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] what the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was already reacting to, and the system carries no intervention. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s own remedy was a sign and not the system, and there is no evidence that the expectation changed what the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] did. Both readings stand. The conclusion rests on the expectation and not on the timing of an alert, and this was a causal factor.

The light vehicle's exit from the spur

The plan required that "Light vehicles shall give way to heavy vehicles at all times and in all circumstances." The driver of LV-118 described slowing at the spur mouth, looking right up the ramp, seeing nothing and driving out at about 25 km/h to turn right. The driver corrected the account on read-back from stopped to slowed and did not believe LV-118 came to a complete stop.

The collision awareness log places LV-118 at the mouth at 02:47:09.2 with the [the other attendee 1] 21.4 m above it, and the impact was 6.2 m into the ramp 2.8 seconds later. The driver's look came a second or two before the [the other attendee 1] came over the crest, when the [the other attendee 1] was beyond anything the driver's position allowed the driver to see. The [the other attendee 1] was inside the driver's 38 m of view from about 02:47:07.4, nearly two seconds before the light vehicle reached the mouth. A stop at the mouth would very probably have shown the [the other attendee 1], and the driver would then probably have let it pass, as the technician did on 04/08/2026.

It is almost certain that driving out without stopping contributed, because without the light vehicle on the ramp there is no collision. The limit is that a stop is only as good as the look from it, at 38 m. This was a causal factor. The light vehicle's movements before the mouth rest on the driver's account alone, and the time the driver left the bore collar, about 02:45, is estimated.

The driver's preparation bore on this. Contractor Management Standard ORR-STD-009 required that the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment "shall be completed at site by every person who will drive a vehicle in an operating pit and shall not be substituted", and made the engaging department responsible for verifying this before a card was issued. The gatehouse issued cards against Hallorn's recognition agreement alone, held no record of the assessment and was not asked for one. The driver's card was issued on 09/08/2026 after a 20 minute briefing on muster points, speed limits and personal protective equipment. The training file shows the Hallorn online module of 24/07/2026, no pit driving assessment and no record of the site-specific supplement. The driver had never seen the traffic management plan.

It is likely that issuing the card without that check contributed, because the driver would not have been carded to drive in an operating pit until the assessment was done, and said that if told to call, the driver would have called. The content of the assessment is [NOT ESTABLISHED: the content of the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment], so what it would have added at the mouth cannot be stated. The driver was already applying the give-way rule, and the plan required no call at an unlisted intersection, so the assessment would not have taught a call at RL 312. This was a causal factor, and the narrower of the conclusions on the light vehicle's side.

Convergence, impact and outcome

The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s response worked. The last steady data point at 02:47:06.0 was 37 km/h, 53 m above the spur mouth, where the survey places the first sight of the beacon. Brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds from 02:47:07.4, with the retarder at maximum and 14 degrees of right steering in the same movement. That was a 1.4 second response, inside the 1.5 seconds the plan's own stopping distance calculation allows. Impact speed was 24 km/h and would have been 37 km/h with no braking, which took about 58 per cent of the impact energy out. The braked scuff deviated 1.4 m to the right away from the open edge, which had a drop of more than 100 m, and the steering kept the push running down the ramp, so the light vehicle came to rest against the pit side windrow. It is very likely that the response reduced the severity of the outcome.

The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] gave the distance at first sight as about forty metres, from memory of a distance seen for a second. The survey puts the beacon in view at 53 m, which is where the download has the [the other attendee 1], and the survey is the measure.

Almost certainly neither driver knew the other was there before that moment. The [the other attendee 1] had no intersection on its screen, no sign on the approach, no call on the channel and no alert. LV-118 came out towards a mouth with 38 m of sight line, no give-way control and no call, and the first sighting available to the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was the beacon over the crest, six seconds before impact. The supervisor did not know a light vehicle was in the pit, and no permit, call-in or record would have told the supervisor. With six seconds left, the convergence almost certainly led directly to the collision.

The impact then followed from the convergence. The [the other attendee 1]'s front left struck the right side of LV-118 at 02:47:12.0 at 24 km/h, with the light vehicle crossing the descending lane to turn right. The damage pattern, the accelerometer reading of 1.9 g and the debris field agree. LV-118 was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp, went over at 11.2 m and came to rest on its left side against the inner windrow. The roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting and was not breached, and the driver's seatbelt was fastened with loading marks on the webbing. The driver sustained a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax and was conscious throughout. With the door on the resting side against the ground, extrication was through the rear. The collision resulted in serious injury to the driver.

The roster and the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s response

The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was on night 10 of a 14 night roster of 18:00 to 06:30, 8 hours 47 minutes into the shift at 02:47 and inside the window of lowest circadian alertness. Every limit in the contractor's fatigue standard was met, and the previous nine shifts were worked in sequence with none extended beyond 12 hours 40 minutes. The roster itself existed and put every [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] at the wheel in that window.

The roster did not contribute to this occurrence. The recorded response was 1.4 seconds, inside the plan's allowance, and the braking and steering were correct and immediate. With braking at the recorded 0.78 m/s2 from 53 m, even a response time of zero would still have ended in a collision, at about 17 km/h instead of 24. The 1.4 seconds cost about 7 km/h of impact speed and not the collision, and no decision or omission on the download is one a roster could have worked through. It was unlikely that the roster influenced the occurrence.

The roster remains a contributory factor in the sense of a standing exposure. It is likely that it increased risk on every swing, because the defence against an unlit hazard at an unlisted intersection is the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s own detection and response. At an intersection with a longer sight line than RL 312, a slower response is the difference between stopping and not.

Fatigue of the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] on the approach (unresolved)

Whether the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was fatigued to a degree that degraded performance during the approach could not be determined either way. The evidence for was the night 10 position, the circadian low and the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s sleep record, which gave 6 hours 30 minutes in the preceding day and between 5 and 7 hours on each of the nine days before, a short recovery repeated across the swing. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] described being tired "the way you are on night ten", and detection in an unlit pit is the task fatigue degrades first.

The evidence against was the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1]'s description of the tiredness as ordinary, "Not falling asleep tired ... I was awake and I was driving properly." Every limit in the fatigue standard was met, and the recorded performance shows none of the usual signs. Being tired on a tenth night is not the same as being fatigued to a degree that degrades performance, and the recorded response argues against that. A detailed fatigue assessment would be needed to settle it. Even if fatigue had been found, the arithmetic above would still show that it did not influence the collision. The matter was not resolved, and nothing from it is carried into the conclusions.

Airborne dust on the ramp (unresolved)

It is likely that airborne dust was present on the ramp above the grade break. The water cart's last pass on that section was at 01:10, 1 hour 37 minutes before the occurrence, against a standing 90 minute interval, so a pass was 7 minutes overdue. The fixed monitor on the RL 328 bench, 180 m up-ramp of the intersection and above the grade break, logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre in the 02:40 to 02:50 interval against a shift mean of 88. The [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] described dust hanging around on the descent and said the cart had been through earlier but "it dries out".

Whether the dust influenced the sighting could not be determined either way. The reading of 142 is well below the site trigger of 250, and it measures particulate at a monitor head and not what could be seen from either cab. Nothing at Bindarra measures visibility. The light vehicle driver was firm that the air was clear, although that account describes the spur below the windrow, with the vehicle slow or stopped, and not the ramp above the crest.

The beacon was in view from 53 m, the first point at which the survey says it could be seen at all, and a 1.4 second response from there is inside the plan's own allowance. A sighting at the geometric limit leaves dust little to explain, and the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] declined to say it made a difference. However, the sighting is inferred from the last steady data point and the survey and was not recorded, so the data cannot exclude dust having cost a fraction of a second at the edge of the [the other attendee 1]'s lights. The matter was not resolved, and nothing from it is carried into the conclusions.

The emergency response

The extrication took 27 minutes. Dispatch stopped Stage 4 traffic 49 seconds after the collision and paged the emergency response team at 02:48. The first response vehicle entered the pit at 02:51 and reached the scene at 02:54. The second responder, who must be present before any extrication begins, is called in from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse and arrived with the hydraulic rescue tool at 03:07. The driver was extricated at 03:14.

The post-incident review found the extrication delayed by approximately 9 minutes, measured from 02:58, when the paramedic's primary survey was complete, to the second responder's arrival. It recorded that the delay did not affect the clinical outcome, because the injuries were stable and the patient was conscious throughout. The collision and the injuries were complete before the team was paged, so it was unlikely that the response time influenced the occurrence or its outcome.

It is very likely that the arrangement is a structural gap that increased risk. The night shift is rostered with one paramedic, and the second responder and the tool come from the village. Nothing in that arrangement scales with the severity of what has happened. It was a contributory factor and not a causal one.

Context for the pattern

The occurrence was not the first of its kind at Bindarra. Four hazard reports raised in the 24 months to 11/08/2026 described a light vehicle and a [the other attendee 1] meeting unexpectedly at an intersection not listed at Appendix B. They included HAZ-2026-0917 and three earlier reports from 03/2025, 09/2025 and 02/2026 at three different locations. All four were closed by the receiving department within three days with an entry that the crew had been reminded to take care and that heavy vehicles have right of way. The closure of HAZ-2026-0917 recorded "Trucks have right of way on the ramp per the traffic management plan." None was referred to the plan owner, and none led to a change to Appendix B, Schedule 1 or any physical control. This pattern does not form a separate factor in this analysis and is given as context for the conditions above.

Conclusions

The investigation identified the following causal and contributory factors. They should not be read as apportioning blame or liability to any organisation or individual.

This investigation applied the standard of proof "Likely or probable": a proposition is established at a probability of 65% or more and not established at 35% or less, and anything between is inconclusive.

Findings

  1. Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14 required the traffic management plan to be reviewed within twelve months and after any significant change to the road network. It defined neither the term nor an example of one, and it set no minimum and no basis for nominating the intersections at which a positive call was required. Bindarra's plan met the guideline on its face and the mine was not in breach. (Safety issue)
  2. Works order WO-26-4471 classified the 240 m RL 312 dewatering spur as routine earthworks under ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3, so no management of change record was raised. None of the three referrals that such a record would have triggered was made, to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the in-cab road network, or the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences. Of the fourteen new Stage 4 roads cut since the last plan review, the three raised under a management of change record were referred and none of the eleven raised under a works order was. (Safety issue)
  3. Site access cards were issued at the gatehouse against the contractor's recognition agreement alone. Neither the site supplement nor the light vehicle pit driving assessment, which ORR-STD-009 clause 7.4 required of every person who would drive in an operating pit, was checked, held or asked for. The light vehicle driver's card was issued without either. (Safety issue)
  4. BIN-TMP-004 required a positive call only at the nine intersections listed at Appendix B. It provided no route for adding an intersection between annual reviews and no requirement to refer a new road to the plan's owner. The RL 312 spur was not listed. (Safety issue)
  5. The S4-LOAD suppression geofence was extended on 09/06/2026 as a system configuration task and carried its boundary up the main ramp to a point 180 m up-ramp of the RL 312 intersection. The collision awareness system raised no alert in the truck at the spur, and the truck operator and the night shift supervisor did not know the system was suppressed on the ramp. (Safety issue)
  6. The RL 312 intersection had no warning sign, no stop or give-way control, no delineation and no posted speed, although the survey gave 41 m of available sight distance against a stopping distance of 96 m. BIN-TMP-004 clause 6.2 required a stop control where the sight distance rule could not be met. (Safety issue)
  7. The available sight distance at the intersection was 41 m against a truck stopping distance of 96 m and a plan minimum of 120 m. The truck operator could first see the light vehicle's beacon at 53 m, and the light vehicle driver at the spur mouth had 38 m of view up the ramp.
  8. Neither the truck operator nor the light vehicle driver made a call before the intersection. BIN-TMP-004 clause 4.3.2 required none because the intersection was not listed at Appendix B.
  9. The light vehicle driver slowed at the spur mouth, looked up the ramp and drove out onto the ramp without coming to a complete stop.
  10. Neither driver knew the other was there until the truck came over the crest, six seconds before the impact.
  11. The truck's front left struck the right side of the light vehicle at 24 km/h. The light vehicle was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side, and the driver sustained a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax.
  12. The truck operator began braking and steering right 1.4 seconds after the beacon came into view, which reduced the impact speed from 37 km/h to 24 km/h.
  13. The truck roster of fourteen consecutive 12.5 hour night shifts met every limit in the contractor's fatigue management standard. (Safety issue)
  14. The night shift extrication capability depended on a second responder and the hydraulic rescue tool being brought from the accommodation village 11 km away. The post-incident review found the extrication delayed by approximately 9 minutes and recorded that the delay did not affect the clinical outcome. (Safety issue)
  15. The ramp surface was dry and the truck's brakes performed to their tested deceleration, so neither was supported as a factor.

Causal factors

  • MSG-14 set no trigger for reviewing the traffic management plan after a significant change and no basis for nominating positive-call intersections. This was virtually certain to have existed. It likely contributed, because a defined trigger would have required the plan to be reopened when a road was added, and a stated basis would have given an intersection failing the sight distance rule a claim on the list. The contribution is held at the standard of proof and no higher. The mine could have held an out-of-cycle review under its own clause 9.1 or listed every intersection without the guideline, so the guideline made doing nothing the default rather than preventing action. (Safety issue)
  • The RL 312 spur was opened under a works order, so nothing was referred to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department or the technical services group. This was virtually certain. It very likely contributed, because a management of change record would have sent the new intersection to the plan's owner and to the group that configured the geofence it was cut inside, and the three roads raised under such a record since the last review were referred. (Safety issue)
  • Access cards were issued with no check of the pit driving assessment. This was virtually certain. It likely contributed, because the assessment would have taught the light vehicle driver to stop and look again at a mouth with no view up the ramp, rather than slow. Evidence against was that the driver already applied the rule that light vehicles give way to heavy vehicles and that the plan required no call at an unlisted intersection, so the assessment would not have taught a call at RL 312. (Safety issue)
  • Positive calls were required only at listed intersections, and intersections were added only at the annual review. This was virtually certain. It very likely contributed, because the truck had called at every listed intersection it passed that night, the last 51 seconds before the collision, and the channel was open with the light vehicle on it. (Safety issue)
  • Collision alerts were suppressed at the spur by a geofence of which operators had no knowledge. This was very likely the case, because the system's configuration and log are documentary, while the operators' lack of knowledge rests on two accounts and the absence of any training record or notice. It likely contributed, because a truck operator who believed the system would sound for a light vehicle on the ramp had one less reason to expect anyone there. An unsuppressed alert would have sounded about half a second after the beacon came into view and about a second before the brakes went on, and the system is advisory only, so any effect was through that expectation and could not be measured. (Safety issue)
  • No stop control or warning sign was provided at an intersection that failed the sight distance rule. This was virtually certain. It likely contributed, because a stop at the spur mouth would very probably have shown the truck to the light vehicle driver, as a week earlier when a dewatering technician reversed into the spur and let a truck pass. The margin from a stop at 38 m was thin, and the effect of a sign on the truck operator rests on that operator's own account. (Safety issue)
  • The sight line of 41 m against a 96 m stopping distance was virtually certain to have existed. It very likely contributed, because with twice the sight line the same 1.4 second response and the same braking would have stopped the truck short of the spur.
  • Neither driver made a positive call before entering the intersection. This was virtually certain. It likely contributed, because a call from either vehicle would have been heard by the other, by dispatch and by the night shift supervisor. A call gives knowledge and not separation, so the vehicles would still have had to resolve who went first.
  • The light vehicle drove out of the spur onto the ramp without stopping. This was virtually certain. It very likely contributed, because without the light vehicle on the ramp there was no collision and the truck was already within the driver's view from the mouth. The look from a stop at 38 m would still have been limited.
  • Neither driver was aware of the other until the truck came over the crest. This was very likely the case, because three independent recordings and all three interviews agree, while the light vehicle's movements before the spur mouth rest on the driver's own account. It very likely contributed, because nothing in the six seconds that remained could have prevented the collision.
  • The truck's front left struck the right side of the light vehicle at 24 km/h, and the light vehicle was pushed 18 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side. Both were virtually certain, and each virtually certainly contributed, because the impact and the roll-over were how the convergence became the driver's injuries.

Contributory factors

  • Truck operators were rostered for fourteen consecutive 12.5 hour night shifts. This was virtually certain. It was unlikely to have contributed to this occurrence, because the download gave a response of 1.4 seconds, inside the 1.5 seconds the plan's stopping distance calculation allows, and braking from 53 m with no response time would still have ended in a collision, at about 17 km/h instead of 24 km/h. It likely increased risk, because the roster places every truck operator at the wheel in the small hours of a tenth, twelfth and fourteenth consecutive night, where the defence against an unlit hazard is the operator's own detection and response. (Safety issue)
  • Night shift extrication waited on a second responder called from the village. This was virtually certain. It was unlikely to have affected this occurrence, because the collision and the injuries were complete before the response was paged and the post-incident review recorded no effect on the clinical outcome. It very likely increased risk on every night shift, because the capability is one paramedic plus a drive from the village and would not scale with a more severe casualty. This matter is carried at the strength recorded so far and not as a settled finding. (Safety issue)

Other findings

  • The truck operator's braking and steering within 1.4 seconds of the beacon coming into view was virtually certain to have occurred. It very likely reduced the severity of the outcome, because the impact speed fell from 37 km/h to 24 km/h and the steering input turned the truck away from the open edge, so the light vehicle came to rest against the pit side windrow.
  • A wet or slippery ramp surface was very unlikely, because the weather record, the surface as examined and the deceleration achieved all agree, and it was not supported as a factor.
  • Reduced service brake performance was very unlikely, because tests eight days before and three days after the occurrence and the occurrence download agreed to within 5 per cent, and it was not supported as a factor.
  • Airborne dust on the ramp above the intersection was likely present, but whether it affected the truck operator's sighting was about as likely as not, so it is not a finding, because the sighting is inferred from the last steady data point and the survey and not recorded, and dust costing a fraction of a second at the edge of the lights could not be excluded or shown.
  • Truck operator fatigue on the approach was about as likely as not to have existed, so it is not a finding, because tiredness on a tenth night is not shown to be fatigue that degrades performance, the recorded response argues against it, and no detailed fatigue assessment was made.

Safety action and recommendations

This section records the action that organisations took after the collision and the recommendations that follow from the safety issues that remain open.

Safety action taken

The Mining Manager of Orrabinda Resources issued a site-wide direction at 05:10 on 12/08/2026, 2 hours 23 minutes after the collision. It requires a positive call on the pit channel before entering any intersection in the Stage 4 pit, whether or not the plan lists it, until further notice. The direction was read at the following four pre-starts and posted beside the Appendix B board in the Stage 4 crib room, and it stands until BIN-TMP-004 is amended. It answers in part the safety issue that positive calls were required only at listed intersections, added only at the annual review. It makes the call a requirement at every intersection for now, but it is a direction and not a change to the plan, so the plan still provides no route by which an intersection reaches Appendix B between annual reviews. The next date on which the RL 312 spur could have been listed under the plan as written was 12/11/2026.

The Mining Manager also had the RL 312 spur barricaded and closed to all traffic on the night of the occurrence, and it remained closed when the action was recorded on 14/08/2026. On that date survey measured the available sight distance at the other ten unlisted roads cut in Stage 4 since the last plan review. Two of the ten were below the clause 6.2 minimum and were closed pending a stop control. This answers in part the safety issue that an intersection failing the sight distance rule had no stop control or warning sign. It removed the hazard at the RL 312 spur and at the two roads found below the minimum, so those two remain open as actions. It did not set a standing requirement for the unlisted roads.

The Technical Services Manager of Tarrowen Mining Services added suppressed proximity events to the monthly collision awareness report on 28/08/2026, broken down by geofence and by vehicle class. The previous twelve months were re-cut on the same basis for the Stage 4 fleet. This is a proactive action and is in progress, with the first report due 30/09/2026. Sixty-eight suppressed proximity events inside the S4-LOAD geofence, nine of them a light vehicle on the main ramp below the boundary, had been recorded in the system throughout and had never been reported to anybody. The action answers in part the safety issue that collision alerts were suppressed at the spur by a geofence that operators knew nothing of. It makes the suppressed events visible to those who receive the report, but it does not tell operators where the system is suppressed, and it does not make a change to a geofence boundary subject to review.

Safety recommendations

Each of the three recommendations below is open, was recorded against the investigator in charge, and has a response due on 30/09/2026.

Works orders that create a new intersection

The spur was opened under works order WO-26-4471, which was classified as routine earthworks, so management of change procedure ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3 excluded it. None of the three referrals that clause 5.4 requires of a management of change record was made. Of the fourteen new roads cut in Stage 4 since the review of 12/11/2025, the three raised under a management of change record were referred to the plan's owner and none of the eleven raised under a works order was. The investigation concluded that it was very likely that this classification contributed to the absence of a stop control and sign, and to the geofence suppression at the spur.

It is recommended that the [the other attendee 1] ensure that a new intersection with a heavy vehicle road cannot be created without the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences each being informed. This could be done by ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3 no longer excluding earthworks that create such an intersection, or by the Schedule 4 works order form carrying the three referrals that clause 5.4 holds.

Route onto the positive-call list between annual reviews

BIN-TMP-004 requires a positive call only at the nine intersections listed at Appendix B. An intersection is added only where it appears on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1, and Schedule 1 is reissued only at the annual review. The plan contains no provision that requires a new road to be referred to its owner when it is cut. The mine's own defence against this interaction therefore could not be armed at the RL 312 intersection by anything anyone did. The evidence showed that the plan made it very likely that no call was made before the spur was entered, because the call was not required there and local practice matched the plan.

It is recommended that the [the other attendee 1] ensure that BIN-TMP-004 provides a route by which an intersection reaches Appendix B between annual reviews, and that the plan requires a new road to be referred to its owner when it is opened to traffic. The next date on which the RL 312 spur could have been listed was 12/11/2026, three months after the collision.

Changes to suppression geofences

The S4-LOAD geofence boundary was moved 180 m up-ramp on 09/06/2026 as a system configuration task. It is not recorded in the traffic management plan, and nobody outside the group that moved it was told. No training record anywhere on site, for any person, covers the geofences. The investigation found that the suppression probably contributed to neither driver being aware of the other, because the [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] took a quiet system on the ramp to mean an empty ramp. The evidence against this was that an unsuppressed alert would have sounded only about a second before the brakes were applied, so the effect rests on expectation and cannot be measured.

It is recommended that the [the other attendee 1] and the contractor ensure that a change to a suppression geofence boundary is treated as a change to a documented control under ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.2, and that operators are told in writing where the collision awareness system is suppressed and why.
